My wife has been unemployed since June with benefits running out this December. I am employed with a base salary of $107k/yr ($2k biweekly after all deductions, 401k, ESPP, insurance, etc.). Health insurance is through my job for both of us. We have $40k in an easily accessible emergency fund. We live in Massachusetts.

 The plan would be to sell the house and net enough to pay for the townhome without a new mortgage. For simplicity’s sake, not taking closing costs, realtor fees, movers, etc. into account: $825k - $246k = $579k - $430k = $149k remainder.

 I'm currently in a PhD program, and making about $2200/month on a graduate stipend. My student loans are in deferment for as long as I'm enrolled in at least 1 credit of research and dissertation. Rent is $1200 but I split it 50/50 with my girlfriend, and after utilities I pay about $750/month. Currently have about $2k split between two credit cards (both with $8k credit limits) and one month of rent in savings in the case of a serious emergency. 
 I have a 2007 Honda CRV that is just absolutely killing me financially. Over the past two years I've had to replace the starter, the alternator, the AC, I've had to get new tires, brakes, I had to get my door lock actuator fixed twice, and now I have an electronical issue that literally prevents me from getting into the vehicle and needs to be fixed at the dealership (which is absurdly expensive). I've spent about $3k on repairs alone this year, maybe $8-10k over the last 4-5 years. 150k miles on it as well. It's just so unreliable.

 I'm starting to think a car payment might be better than dropping $1-2k multiple times a year on a car that is absolutely failing.  I guess I'm just looking for general advice here. Should I keep looking? Is this whole idea completely stupid and unfeasible? Is this the right move (and if so, what steps should I take?)
 This is all completely new to me and I'm still trying to figure things out. I figured you guys would be willing to provide a reality check if this isn't feasible.

text:
New Job Offer - ESOP plan question, what's your take on this structure?

Have you ever seen anything like this? What's your take? This offer is important to me because I am planning to move my family of four to a new state, and this company is my preferred company of the three offers I have. While ESOPs are not common on the whole, they're pretty common in my industry. I have seen many offers with them. 
 In my experience, usually the company treats them as separate from the 401k retirement match. i.e. they will contribute, for example, 100% match to 3% for 401k and they contribute a separate discretionary % to the ESOP.
 For this new offer the employee has no "control" over where the company "match" goes. Example, one year it could be 1% 401k, 3% ESOP. The next it could be 0% 401k, 4% ESOP. The next it could be 4% 401k, 0% ESOP. So there is no guaranteed company 401k match. Also, the 4% is non-elective. So, if I put 0% into my 401k (I would not), the company would still contribute 4% if it was one of those 100% 401k years.
 I have hesitation about concentrated risk in the ESOP. However, I will be fully funding two ROTH IRAs, an HSA, and nearly maxing my employee 401k contributions. So it's not like my retirement is entirely dependent on the ESOP, which is why I could see it being okay.

text:
Term insurance online vs through an agent: is the cheaper online premium actually the same product?

This question keeps coming up here, so putting down what I understand and asking for corrections.
 Same insurer, same plan, online is often cheaper. Partly because there is no agent commission, partly because some insurers price online-only variants differently. The cover is identical if the plan name and features match.
 What actually decides the claim is not the channel:
 - Full disclosure on the proposal form (tobacco, alcohol, conditions, other policies). Non-disclosure is the most common reason claims get contested.
 - Medical underwriting. If tests are offered, take them.
 - Correct, up-to-date nominee details.
 - Section 45 makes a policy incontestable on most grounds after 3 years.
 Where an agent helps: filling the proposal correctly, and supporting the nominee at claim time. Where online helps: lower premium, no push towards ROP or endowment, and documents arriving instantly.
 Some insurers sell term only online (Acko Life is one), while most traditional insurers sell the same plans both ways.
 IRDAI also requires death claims that do not need investigation to be settled within 15 days of complete documents. Has anyone been through a claim on an online-bought policy? Did the channel make any difference?

text:
Car Loan Dillemma (USA, CA)

I'm in a dilemma, bit of a doozy this post is. I currently have a car with a loan on it, around $3600 principal remaining on the loan/another 13 months left of payments. The car runs, but the transmission is beginning to slip, and has always had an parasitic drain that has been problematic and unable to be diagnosed. I've also exceeded in mileage the projected lifespan of this model. So all this to say, I began searching for a new car. Initially, I wanted to at least keep this car until it was paid off, but there have been times where a powertrain light randomly comes on, or there are very drastically different starting noises, that which seem to indicate larger problems and have left me uncomfortable with the idea of relying on this car for another year.
 I work at a financial institution, we get an interest rate discount for credit products. I do not care for this job and am only staying until I land something better/finish school. The Fed has also raised, and there is talk of more interest rate hikes to follow. I also have a sudden extraneous recent financial strain and to keep my bills paid am now running a higher credit card balance. With all this coming into play, I figured that if I want to get another auto loan, the time may as well be now, while I can take advantage of an industry rate discount, and before my credit potentially drops.
 I found a vehicle, and funded the loan for the new car. I was initially going to trade in my current car and roll the negative equity into my new loan, but I was deterred by this from many different sources and people around me, suggesting instead to get a personal loan, pay off the car, and sell it privately now that I'd have title. The negative equity would have been ~3k, and according to KBB I should be able to sell it for 5-6k private party.
 The new car's payment is not due until this month. After funding my car loan I got a personal loan for old car payoff as well as the extraneous situation that had been costing me. However, the other situation is becoming much worse than I feared, and I may have to use the entire personal loan to address it, the loan being for 7k. So no money for the old car payoff.
 Still determined to stick to my plan of selling the car, I received counsel from different sources to pay off the car with my credit card. Not ideal, but once I sell the car, I can just put the proceeds directly back to the credit card.
 Well I counted on this option, went to my auto loan's portal, and attempted to schedule a card payment through the lender's third-party server (specifically for card payments) and found out that they do not accept credit card payments, only debit.
 I live paycheck to paycheck, HCOL area. I do not have savings. So suffice to say I do not have the old car's payoff amount in any cash equivalent.
 If I cannot pay this car off I will be stuck with two car payments which I flat out cannot afford, especially with this additional monthly payment for the 7k personal loan.
 It has been 6 days until I purchased the car (USA, CA). Is it too late for me to back out of the sale? Or the loan? If I can cancel on the loan, will the dealer at least potentially buy back the car for the same price?
 Have no idea what to do, time is running out. Feel like I fucked myself over big time.

text:
Looking for second eyes on long-term plan

I am 34, planning out my next 15 years roughly.
 At 49, my employer contribution maxes out, and my house is paid off. I want to put myself in a strong position to be financially independent, or close to it by 49, and ready to retire at 55 when my employer pension can kick in for 50k/year.
 Currently, making roughly $140k pre tax. House worth 405k at purchase, 260k left on mortgage.
 Zero TFSA, 30k in RRSP. Once all is said and done, I'm able to reliably save 10k, which I'm currently putting into my RRSP and investing in standard ETF funds. 70k contribution room in RRSP, 100k in TFSA.
 First step I'm considering is a Smith maneuver. Open a HELOC, with roughly 64k limit. Take out maybe 50k, invest it in a variety of Canadian bank and energy sector stocks, net maybe 4% dividends plus growth, take the dividends and tax break from HELOC interest and use them to pay off the mortgage faster, end of year take another 10k from the HELOC and invest, leave the interest coming from the remaining HELOC room. I did a spreadsheet for this, using 6.5% HELOC interest, paying taxes on dividends at 18.5% and recouping taxes in HELOC interest at 36% tax bracket. Using that math, I need only an average 1% growth on the stocks over the next 11 years to break even.
 After that I would reassess and possibly divert the dividend payments to the HELOC to slowly lower that until 55. Depending on the actual value of the account, I could retire without my pension yet, and use the low income years to sell off stocks and avoid most CAP-Gains.

text:
I’m 30 and stuck in a cycle of working hard, saving money, and losing it all. How do I break it?

I’m 30 years old and work abroad on shipyard projects. I usually spend several months away from home, working long hours and sacrificing my social life to save money.
 The problem is that almost every year, I seem to repeat the same financial mistakes.
 I work hard abroad, save a decent amount, then return home for the summer. I take some time off, enjoy life, and tell myself I’ll find a job soon. But the weeks go by, I don’t earn enough, and my savings slowly disappear.
 This summer was probably the worst example. I returned home in early May and didn’t start working until about six weeks later. Even then, I was only getting a couple of shifts per week. I knew my savings were running low, but I kept spending, thinking I’d just make the money back on my next project abroad.
 Eventually, I ran out of money and even had to borrow some from close friends.
 I also have a few thousand in cryptocurrency investments, but they’re currently at a loss, and I’m reluctant to sell them just to cover my expenses.
 Now I’m back abroad, working again, and I can’t stop thinking about how I could have started this winter with €3–4k saved instead of practically starting from scratch.
 What frustrates me most isn’t just losing the money. It’s the fact that I keep repeating the same cycle.
 Work hard, save money, come home, spend too much, run out of savings, go abroad again, and start all over.
 I’m tired of feeling like all those months away from home were for nothing. I don’t want to spend the next five or ten years living this way.
 I know I need better financial discipline, but I also want to enjoy my time at home instead of working constantly.
 Has anyone else been stuck in a similar cycle? What actually helped you break it? How did you learn to enjoy your life without constantly destroying your financial progress?
 I’d really appreciate advice, especially from people who work seasonal jobs or spend months working abroad.
